name: Malabar Spinach
variety: Species-level edible Malabar spinach identity; cultivar unspecified
summary: A heat-loving climbing leafy vegetable, botanically distinct from true spinach (Spinacia oleracea). This identity represents Basella alba, not the red-stemmed ornamental Basella rubra.

identity.guidance: POWO accepts Basella alba in Basellaceae. UF/IFAS distinguishes B. alba, typically dark-green and edible, from B. rubra, often grown ornamentally for colored stems; the entry does not specify a cultivar.

cultivation.short: Warm-weather vine; maintain moisture for tender leaves
cultivation.guidance: UF/IFAS reports optimal growth at ambient temperatures of at least 80°F and says growth slows below 80°F; frost is not tolerated. It recommends continuous moisture for leaf quality and reports that dry conditions can make leaves bitter and promote flowering. This is Florida crop guidance, not a hydroponic recipe.

growth.short: Climbing vine that benefits from support and periodic pruning
growth.guidance: UF/IFAS reports vines can reach six feet or longer and recommends a trellis or fence, with pruning of leaves and overlong vines to maintain the desired form. Full sun is tolerated, while partial shade may produce larger, more succulent leaves; the current structured light vocabulary cannot express that preference without overclaiming a single category.

harvest.guidance: UF/IFAS describes leaves and young stems as the marketable parts and reports maturity around 70 days from seed under optimal conditions. That regional estimate is not a guaranteed schedule for every garden or seed lot.

problems.short: Cold, dry conditions, and selected leaf pests are documented concerns
problems.guidance: UF/IFAS reports frost sensitivity, reduced leaf quality and flowering under moisture stress, and possible fungal leaf spots, snails, and nematodes. These are source-reported risks, not a complete diagnosis or a claim that every plant will be affected.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: UF/IFAS field and garden guidance does not establish performance in a home recirculating hydroponic system.

growthHabits.reason: The source describes a climbing vine, but the current controlled vocabulary has no climbing value; the prose retains the sourced habit without forcing a different category.

evidence.note: The source says the vine can grow six feet or longer; this is not a cultivar-specific maximum.

spread.reason: The source gives no supported mature spread.

spacing.reason: UF/IFAS bed and transplant distances are outdoor crop guidance, not indoor pod spacing.

light.reason: UF/IFAS says full sun is tolerated but partial shade may improve leaf size and succulence; a single requirement category would erase that distinction.

name: Yardlong Bean
variety: Yardlong / asparagus-bean crop group within Vigna unguiculata; cultivar unspecified
summary: A warm-season climbing cowpea grown mainly for long, tender pods. It is taxonomically within Vigna unguiculata and is kept distinct from common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) and dry cowpea identities.

identity.short: POWO subspecies: Vigna unguiculata subsp. sesquipedalis
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Vigna unguiculata subsp. sesquipedalis and records Vigna sesquipedalis as a synonym. UF/IFAS uses the crop name long bean and describes its distinctive climbing pod crop; this record does not identify a named cultivar.

cultivation.short: Warm-season climbing crop; cold and waterlogging impair growth
cultivation.guidance: UF/IFAS reports best growth in warm conditions and tolerance of heat and drought, with adverse effects from waterlogging, cold, and frost. Its Florida soil pH and field-management recommendations are regional agronomy and are not converted into container or nutrient prescriptions.

growth.guidance: UF/IFAS reports vines can reach 9–12 feet and recommends trellising; its six-foot trellis and bed spacing describe field production. No indoor footprint or hydroponic support design is established.

harvest.guidance: UF/IFAS describes long bean as a repeatedly harvested crop in Florida and recommends picking immature pods while tender; harvest timing varies with location and season. Its reported field calendar is not presented as a universal days-to-harvest value.

problems.short: Avoid cold, frost, and waterlogged soil
problems.guidance: UF/IFAS identifies cold, frost, and waterlogging as growth risks and reports powdery mildew under very humid south Florida summer conditions. The disease note is regional and does not imply cultivar-specific susceptibility.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Open-field long-bean production evidence does not establish home hydroponic suitability.

growthHabits.reason: The source supports climbing vines, but climbing is not a value in the current controlled growth-habit vocabulary.

evidence.note: Reported crop vines reach 9–12 feet; this is a regional crop range, not a named cultivar guarantee.

spread.reason: No mature spread is supplied for this unspecified cultivar group.

spacing.reason: Florida field bed and plant spacing do not establish indoor or pod spacing.

light.reason: The selected source supports warmth and climbing habit but does not provide a defensible outdoor sun category or indoor grow-light tier.

name: Bitter Melon
variety: Species-level crop identity; Chinese and Indian horticultural types are distinct, cultivar unspecified
summary: A tropical and subtropical climbing cucurbit harvested for its unripe fruit. UF/IFAS cautions that it may escape cultivation in Florida; this species-level entry does not represent a particular Chinese or Indian type.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Momordica charantia in Cucurbitaceae. UF/IFAS distinguishes Chinese and Indian horticultural types by fruit form; no such type or named cultivar is assigned to this general identity.

cultivation.short: Warm, moist conditions support slow-germinating seed and vigorous vines
cultivation.guidance: UF/IFAS describes a thick, hard seed coat and usually slow germination; warm, moist soil (60–95°F in the source) is required, while dry or too-cool soil can delay or prevent emergence. Its Florida planting calendar is regional and should not be generalized to other climates.

growth.short: Climbing vine; provide support and allow for insect pollination outdoors
growth.guidance: UF/IFAS reports vines up to 16 feet and recommends trellis support for production. Separate male and female flowers and insect-mediated cross-pollination are described; low pollinator activity can limit fruit set. These outdoor crop details do not establish compatibility with indoor systems.

harvest.short: Harvest the fruit while green or slightly yellow
harvest.guidance: UF/IFAS recommends harvesting unripe green or slightly yellow fruit; overmature fruit turns orange and may open to release seeds. Its approximate 50-day harvest reference is explicitly for north Florida and is not a universal maturity claim.

problems.short: Manage to prevent escape from cultivation
problems.guidance: UF/IFAS assigns the species a Florida status of Caution—Manage to Prevent Escape because it may establish and spread outside cultivation. This is a Florida-specific ecological warning, not a universal legal designation. The source also notes slow emergence from hard seed coats and the need for pollination for fruit set.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Florida outdoor cucurbit guidance does not establish home recirculating hydroponic suitability.

growthHabits.reason: The source supports climbing habit, but the current controlled vocabulary has no climbing value.

evidence.note: UF/IFAS says vines may reach 16 feet; it is a regional species-level crop description, not a cultivar-specific guarantee.

spread.reason: No supported mature spread is supplied.

spacing.reason: Florida field row and plant spacing are not indoor pod spacing.

light.reason: The selected source does not establish a precise outdoor exposure category or indoor light requirement.

name: Peanut
variety: Species-level cultivated peanut identity; botanical market type and cultivar unspecified
summary: A warm-season legume with an unusual fruiting cycle: flowers form above ground, then pegs carry developing pods into the soil. This is a species-level entry, not a named peanut type or cultivar.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Arachis hypogaea in Fabaceae. UF/IFAS recognizes runner, Spanish, Virginia, and Valencia market types; no market type or cultivar is implied by this species-level profile.

cultivation.short: Warm-season crop with loose soil for underground pod development
cultivation.guidance: UF/IFAS recommends planting raw peanuts after frost danger in its Florida context and describes loose, prepared garden soil. The crop's pegs must enter soil for pods to develop; the page does not establish a hydroponic method. Regional planting dates and maturity vary by peanut type.

growth.short: Low-growing annual; flowers above ground and matures pods underground
growth.guidance: UF/IFAS describes peanut as a low-growing, self-pollinating annual. After flowering, a peg grows downward into the soil and the pod develops underground. This geocarpic lifecycle is the key management distinction from above-ground pod legumes.

harvest.short: Dig the plant and cure pods after they mature
harvest.guidance: UF/IFAS describes lifting plants and curing pods after harvest; timing differs among market types and conditions. Its maturity examples are type-specific and are not assigned to this cultivar-unspecified identity. Iowa State's home-garden page also warns that its 1997 guidance may not be current, so it is used only as corroborating context.

problems.short: Keep the fruiting zone workable and verify locally appropriate crop practices
problems.guidance: Iowa State Extension notes loose soil is needed for peg penetration and shallow cultivation is advised to avoid root damage; UF/IFAS notes pests and diseases in production settings. Because some source recommendations are regional or older, this profile does not prescribe crop-protection products or a universal fertilizer program.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The crop requires pegs and pods to develop in soil; hydroponic production is not established by the selected home-garden sources.

evidence.note: UF/IFAS describes low-growing plants; exact habit varies among market types.

height.reason: UF/IFAS describes low-growing plants but gives no general mature height for an unspecified type.

spread.reason: Habit differs among peanut types and no species-wide spread is selected.

spacing.reason: Spacing varies by market type; cited field/garden rows do not define container or pod spacing.

light.reason: The selected sources do not provide a directly usable outdoor exposure classification or indoor grow-light requirement.

name: Common Purslane
variety: Species-level edible common purslane identity; cultivar unspecified; not moss rose (P. grandiflora)
summary: A succulent-leaved plant grown as an edible cut-and-come-again green, but also a persistent garden weed. Distinct from ornamental moss rose (Portulaca grandiflora); manage seed set and stem fragments to limit unwanted spread.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Portulaca oleracea in Portulacaceae. UF/IFAS and UW–Madison Extension distinguish common purslane from ornamental moss rose (P. grandiflora); this entry represents the edible species, not a named crop cultivar.

cultivation.short: Warm-weather crop; moisture supports tender leaf quality
cultivation.guidance: UF/IFAS describes moist, well-drained growing conditions with sun for Florida production; UW Extension says the species grows in full sun and warm weather and prefers regular water for more palatable leaves. The guidance applies to the species/crop, not a particular upright commercial cultivar.

growth.short: Low, spreading succulent; prevent unwanted reseeding
growth.guidance: UW Extension describes a mostly prostrate mat that may spread widely and notes that mature plants produce many seeds; stems can root at nodes if left on moist soil. As this species can be a persistent weed, container or bed cultivation should include monitoring for seed release and unwanted spread.

harvest.short: Cut tender stems before they become fibrous
harvest.guidance: UW Extension reports harvest in about 6–8 weeks and supports whole-plant harvest or cutting stems back for regrowth. UF/IFAS recommends tender young stems before flowering in its Florida crop guide. Timing and repeat interval vary with growing conditions.

problems.short: Control escape, seed set, and unwanted stem rooting
problems.guidance: UW Extension notes seeds can remain viable in soil for decades and cut stems may root at nodes; it also identifies occasional purslane sawfly and leafminer weevil damage. UF/IFAS likewise discusses purslane as a weed as well as a possible crop. These points support containment, not a claim of universal pest pressure.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Outdoor edible-crop guidance does not establish suitability or containment behavior in a recirculating home system.

evidence.note: UW Extension describes mostly prostrate stems and a mat that can spread up to three feet in its regional species profile.
UW Extension reports plants may reach 16 inches depending on moisture; this is species-level outdoor context, not a named cultivar specification.
UW Extension describes a mat covering up to three feet in diameter; this is not a cultivated cultivar guarantee.

spacing.reason: Garden-bed spacing is not an indoor pod-spacing recommendation.

evidence.note: UW Extension states that common purslane grows in full sun; this is outdoor exposure, not indoor grow-light intensity.
